findings.title: Cap-exceeded path commits partial deletes then raises, losing the count and reporting false failure
findings.evidence: Each DELETE is followed by db.commit() (line 36); the for/else raises RuntimeError when the final executed batch was full. If matching rows >= MAX_BATCHES*batch_size, up to 1000*500=500,000 rows are deleted and committed, then the function raises and the 'deleted' tally is never returned to the caller, who sees a failure despite committed deletions. It also raises falsely when the table holds exactly 1000 full batches and is fully drained.
findings.recommendation: Do not commit the batch that trips the cap, or include the deleted count in the exception/return a partial result. Decide 'more rows remain' before committing (e.g. stop and return when the previous batch was full and MAX_BATCHES reached), so the caller always learns how many rows were actually removed.

findings.title: WHERE guard only rejects empty/whitespace, so a constant-true or injected fragment passes
findings.evidence: The mandatory-filter check is just: if not where_sql or not where_sql.strip(). A caller passing where_sql='1=1' (or any request-derived fragment) passes the guard and the f-string interpolates it directly into DELETE ... WHERE {where_sql} LIMIT ?, enabling full-table batched deletion or SQL injection if the trusted-caller contract is violated anywhere.
findings.evidence_quote: if not where_sql or not where_sql.strip():
findings.recommendation: Enforce the contract structurally where feasible (e.g. accept a column/operator/value spec and build the clause, or reject constant-true clauses), and add a lint/test asserting where_sql is never sourced from request input.

findings.title: Loop correctness depends on cursor.rowcount being the true delete count
findings.evidence: Control flow uses deleted += cursor.rowcount and if cursor.rowcount < batch_size: break. DB-API permits -1 when rowcount is unavailable; under such a driver the first batch would add -1, satisfy the < batch_size break immediately, and silently stop after one batch while reporting -1. This is driver-dependent and safe under sqlite3, where rowcount is accurate for DELETE.
findings.recommendation: Guard against a negative rowcount (e.g. treat <0 as an error rather than a break signal) or derive the affected count in a driver-independent way.

findings.title: matching field has different meaning in dry run versus real run
findings.evidence: Dry run returns matching = pre-delete SELECT COUNT(*), while the real run returns matching = deleted (the two are equal only when everything matched was actually removed). Callers comparing dry-run blast radius to the real result can be misled.
findings.recommendation: Rename or split the fields so dry-run pre-count and actual deleted count are unambiguous (e.g. 'would_delete' vs 'deleted').
